A magistrate judge ruled in favor of Apple in its effort to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies as part of its defense against the Department of Justice's antitrust lawsuit. Here's the full story.

A bit of background

Last May, Apple asked the court presiding over the DOJ's 2024 antitrust case against it to compel the following 14 federal agencies to turn over documents related to their evaluation, procurement, and use of smartphones and wearable devices:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

Apple argued in its request that the records might help support its defense against allegations that its iPhone policies are anticompetitive.

In short, Apple's argument was that if federal agencies chose its products based on their security, privacy, or other features, that would support its position that those practices represent legitimate product advantages rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

The government pushed back on Apple's request, arguing that the agencies are not parties to the case, do not regulate smartphones, and that their procurement or use is different from that of typical consumers.

It asked the court to quash the subpoenas, arguing they were both irrelevant and unduly burdensome, and that they could implicate privileged, confidential, or national security-sensitive material.

The court subsequently referred the dispute to retired federal judge Jose Linares, who is serving as a special master for discovery and will decide whether Apple can enforce the subpoenas.

In complex cases with significant discovery disputes, courts sometimes appoint special masters to handle narrower disputes, reducing the workload on the presiding judge. Special masters can be retired judges, practicing attorneys, or other experts with relevant experience.

Apple gets to seek documents from the federal agencies

Judge Linares has now ruled in Apple's favor, finding that all of its document requests are relevant to the core claims in the case. He also said the government failed to provide sufficient justification for its broader objections.

Although the special master ruled in Apple's favor, that doesn't mean Apple will immediately receive all the documents it requested.

Instead, the agencies can still withhold specific records they believe are privileged or otherwise protected, but they must identify those records on a privilege log. Any disputes over those assertions could trigger another round of discovery disputes, including potentially in-camera review by Judge Linares.
